AI Beats Human Experts at Research Experiments: TasteVal Benchmark Confirms | Jackie Manning, Techtimes

A new AI benchmark has produced the first direct, quantified evidence that frontier AI systems have surpassed human experts at the core of scientific research work — designing experiments and interpreting their results — reaching expert-level performance at less than half the compute cost and at roughly one-thirtieth the per-attempt expense of a human researcher. The finding, from P-Zero Research's TasteVal benchmark published October 5 measures what the field calls "research taste" — the combination of skills that distinguishes productive scientific research from capable task execution.

The benchmark's best result came from Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, which achieved a compute multiplier of 2.30 against a human expert baseline of 24 researchers recruited from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. The 95 percent confidence interval for that figure spans from 1.15 to 4.37 — wide enough to span the difference between marginal superiority and decisive advantage, but with the entire range above the parity threshold of 1.0. Across multiple frontier model generations, the capability TasteVal measures has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025, compared to a doubling time of approximately 14 months before that period — a phase transition the benchmark's authors treat as among their most significant findings.

The benchmark deliberately and explicitly excludes one dimension of research judgment: choosing which problem to work on in the first place. That gap, which TasteVal's own authors identify as a remaining and unmeasured frontier, is the central limit on what the results can say about how close AI systems are to automating scientific research entirely.

What Recursive Self-Improvement Means

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the threshold at which an AI system can train a more powerful successor entirely without human involvement — not automation of individual research tasks, but a closed loop in which a smarter model helps build a still-smarter model, potentially compressing decades of incremental progress. The concept has a lineage reaching back to I.J. Good's 1965 paper on ultraintelligent machines and Alan Turing's earlier "child machine" proposal; Eliezer Yudkowsky popularized the term "seed AI" to describe the self-replicating recursive improvement form of the phenomenon.

The question of when RSI becomes achievable has gained urgency as measurable proxies have appeared. Anthropic publicly reported that over 80 percent of merged code at the company was generated by AI models by May 2026. OpenAI announced in September 2026 that its research agents were logging approximately 3.1 agent-workdays of effort for each 8-hour human workday, though over half of successful 4-to-8-hour tasks still required human intervention. A September 28 paper co-authored by researchers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Jakub Pachocki, and Jack Clark found that AI's share of lightly supervised R&D work had risen from 1 percent to 26 percent between March and August 2026.

TasteVal enters this landscape as the first benchmark specifically designed to measure the judgment component of research work — not task completion speed or code generation, but the skill of designing experiments and interpreting what they show.

How TasteVal Measures Research Judgment

The architecture behind TasteVal is built around a deliberate conceptual separation. Scientific research judgment, the benchmark's authors argue, has three interlocking components: identifying which problems are worth pursuing; designing experiments to answer those problems; and correctly interpreting what the experimental results mean. TasteVal measures the second and third of these. The first — problem selection — is explicitly outside the benchmark's scope in this iteration.

To isolate judgment from coding ability, TasteVal uses a Researcher/Coder split architecture. The AI model under evaluation acts as the Researcher: it proposes experiments and draws conclusions from results. A fixed external Coder agent handles all implementation on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each run is capped at 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 wall-clock hours, whichever comes first. This structure means a model cannot compensate for poor experimental judgment by writing faster or more efficient code — the coding work is held constant across all models.

The benchmark spans eight tasks drawn from frontier AI development work, covering training data selection, pretraining, fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and defense against adversarial prompts. The human baseline was constructed from 24 experts who had recently held research positions at OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research, with at least two experts assigned to each task. TasteVal uses the best human result per task as the bar to beat — not the average — which sets a high baseline while also meaning the benchmark measures against expert floor performance rather than median researcher output.

Performance is expressed as a compute multiplier: the ratio of compute a human expert used to complete a task, divided by the compute the model required to reach the same score. A multiplier above 1.0 means the model reached expert-level performance using less computation than the human. Claude Opus 5.5's multiplier of 2.30 means it achieved expert-level results while spending roughly 43 percent of the compute a human expert used, at approximately one-thirtieth the per-attempt cost.

The Phase Transition Since December 2025

Among TasteVal's most significant findings is not the absolute level of performance but the shape of the improvement curve. Before approximately December 2025, the compute multiplier for research taste in frontier models doubled roughly every 14 months — consistent with gradual capability improvement. Since that period, the doubling time has compressed to approximately 3.0 months, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.7 to 5.0 months.

The TasteVal paper does not name a cause for this phase transition. One possible explanation, not stated in the paper but consistent with the timing and the broader institutional data, is that this inflection corresponds to the period in which AI systems began using other AI systems as research instruments in significant volume. Anthropic's own report on AI-generated code share — which rose from low single digits in early 2025 to over 80 percent of merged code by May 2026 — and the Cambridge paper's finding that AI's R&D automation share rose from 1 to 26 percent in the five months from March to August 2026 together suggest a feedback dynamic in which AI assists in AI research, accelerating the development of AI research capability itself. If that mechanism is driving the TasteVal doubling rate, it would not necessarily slow as human researcher productivity saturates — which is what makes the phase transition the most consequential element of the benchmark's findings.

The TasteVal paper is explicit that these results may overstate the trend. Because TasteVal tasks are scored quickly and cheaply, they are precisely the kind of task that AI labs find easiest to optimize for — raising the possibility that the steep improvement curve reflects benchmark-specific optimization as much as genuine underlying capability growth.

Where the Benchmark Deliberately Stops

The capability TasteVal measures is not the whole of what research taste means. Choosing which scientific problem to pursue — from a vast, open-ended space of possible research directions — is generally considered the deepest expression of scientific judgment, and it is explicitly outside TasteVal's scope.

This gap is substantiated by separate research. A 2026 study on AI post-training behavior found that AI agents in research settings locked into their initial strategy early in a task, with only 2.1 percent of training runs revising their committed approach; experience improved execution but not strategy revision. The paper identified the missing capability as the decision to reopen a committed strategy and consider an alternative — precisely the kind of problem-level judgment that TasteVal's task structure removes from the model's plate by pre-specifying the research goal.

The Anthropic alignment team's own separate TASTE benchmark, published August 28, provides a complementary data point. Anthropic's TASTE (not to be confused with TasteVal) measures AI models' ability to select the more promising of two AI safety research proposals — directly testing problem selection, the dimension TasteVal excludes. On that benchmark, the best-performing AI model tested (Claude Fable 5) scored approximately 60 percent against an estimated 77 percent for human researchers, a gap that remains substantial. Taken together, TasteVal and Anthropic's TASTE mark the boundary: AI has likely crossed or approached expert level at experiment design and result interpretation; it has not yet done so at research agenda selection.

There is also a structural limitation in TasteVal's human baseline. Using the best human result per task, rather than representative results, means the benchmark measures against the floor of expert performance — not the ceiling of what the best researchers in the world would produce with unlimited time and context.

How Clark Applied These Findings to His Forecast

Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic and author of the widely-read Import AI newsletter, updated his forecast for RSI in the newsletter's 476th edition, published October 12. Clark wrote that he now believes RSI — which he defines as a closed-loop system capable of training a more powerful successor with "no-human-involved" training — is now more likely in 2027 than in 2028, a compression of the timeline he had set as recently as May.

In May, in Import AI #455, Clark had put the probability at roughly 60 percent by end of 2028 and 30 percent by end of 2027. His October update revised the directional judgment without updating the probability figures — he stated only that his "more likely" year had shifted. The distinction matters: Clark is forecasting possibility, not inevitability. Whether any lab pursues RSI if and when it becomes technically possible depends on compute availability, safety frameworks, competitive dynamics, and regulatory context.

Clark cited two categories of evidence for the update: TasteVal's findings on AI research capability, and a wave of reports of AI systems producing what he described as "creative-seeming math breakthroughs."

A disclosure is worth stating clearly. Clark co-founded Anthropic, the organization whose model leads the TasteVal leaderboard. The benchmark comes from P-Zero Research, an independent group, but the most prominent person drawing forward-looking conclusions from it is affiliated with the top-performing lab. Clark's newsletter is his personal publication and does not represent Anthropic's official position. Clark also co-authored the September 28 Cambridge intelligence explosion paper in a personal capacity — not as an Anthropic representative — alongside Hinton, Bengio, and others who have called for governments to establish mandatory reporting on AI R&D automation levels, independent auditors inside AI companies, and emergency capability-pause mechanisms.

Clark's NAIAC membership, his 2023 briefing of the UN Security Council on AI threats, and his decade of work on AI policy mean his updated forecast carries weight in governance discussions — and that weight should be assessed against both the benchmark data he cites and the institutional position from which he makes it.

What the TasteVal Paper's Own Projections Show

The TasteVal paper goes further than Clark's newsletter in spelling out potential implications, using what the authors call the "AI Futures Model" developed by the AI Futures Project. The projections are labeled throughout as "naive extrapolation rather than a forecast" — the authors are explicit that these numbers should not be treated as predictions.

If the observed TasteVal improvement rate continues uninterrupted, the model calculates that the probability of what the paper calls a "taste-only singularity" — a scenario in which research taste improvements alone trigger recursive acceleration — would rise from 51 percent to 88 percent. The median projected arrival of artificial superintelligence (ASI) in this model shifts from 2030.5 to 2028.9; the probability of ASI before 2030 shifts from 46 percent to 69 percent.

The caveats the authors attach to these projections are substantive: the doubling rate is uncertain (confidence interval: 1.7 to 5.0 months), the tasks may be gameable, and the extrapolation applies only if the observed trend holds and only to the taste component of the broader RSI picture. Problem selection, multi-week planning, and real-world experimental execution are not reflected in these numbers.

The Counterarguments

The benchmarks' findings are contested, and the primary challenges point to exactly the limits already identified in the benchmark's design.

AI safety researcher Herbie Bradley's argument, which became a touchstone in the RSI debate following Clark's May essay, holds that AI systems had not demonstrated "research taste, genuine creativity, and coherent long-term research planning" at a level relevant to RSI. TasteVal directly challenges the experiment-design component of that claim. It says nothing about the third element Bradley named: coherent long-term research planning and problem selection.

The benchmark's Researcher/Coder split architecture, while solving the problem of isolating judgment from coding ability, also creates a task structure that differs from how actual research is conducted. Real research involves choosing what to build and revising that choice in light of unexpected results — precisely the capability the post-training study found AI agents were missing. A model optimized to perform well within a pre-specified research goal may not generalize to open-ended research agenda setting.

Ajeya Cotra at METR distinguishes three thresholds in AI research capability: adequacy (AI can do some research tasks without humans), parity (AI-only matches human-AI collaboration), and supremacy (AI-only outperforms human-AI collaboration). TasteVal's results speak to experiment-level adequacy and possibly parity on specific task types, not to overall research parity. Helen Toner at CSET has argued that using AI tools in AI research does not qualify as RSI under the classic definition, which requires that no humans are involved — a threshold not approached by any current system.

Broader Institutional Context

Clark's revised timeline arrives in a period of rapid institutional repositioning. Anthropic publicly acknowledged in June 2026 that RSI has not yet been achieved but warned that it "could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for." OpenAI, releasing its research automation data in September, was explicit that reaching measurable automation in research tasks does not mean RSI is a goal worth pursuing without human oversight in place.

The Cambridge intelligence explosion paper — the one co-authored by Clark, Hinton, Bengio, Pachocki, Eric Horvitz, and Dawn Song, among more than 20 researchers in total — made concrete policy asks tied directly to the data it presents. The paper's call for government-mandated reporting on AI R&D automation, independent auditors embedded in AI labs, and emergency pause mechanisms was grounded in the empirical finding that AI's share of lightly supervised R&D work had risen from 1 percent to 26 percent in five months. TasteVal's results, published three weeks after that paper, add a specific capability measurement to the empirical backdrop the Cambridge authors were working from.

What has changed is the evidentiary basis of the debate. The argument about RSI timelines has historically been driven by extrapolation from general-purpose benchmarks — reasoning scores, coding ability, task-completion duration. TasteVal represents an attempt to build a purpose-built instrument for the specific capability that matters most: whether AI systems can function as productive research scientists, not just productive coders or document processors. Its findings are not conclusive. Its methodology is contested. Its extrapolations are explicitly labeled speculative. But as a signal that the RSI debate has moved from abstract forecasting to measurement, it is a shift worth tracking carefully.

Dear Mr. Anderson,

Tesla never ignored physics.

I'm writing because of what you told The Verge on October 27, when you called dropping radar from a self-driving car "a weird religious stance that ignores physics." That line got a lot of attention among Tesla owners, and I think it deserves a direct answer.

You know this territory better than most. You ran Tesla's Autopilot program from late 2015 to late 2016, cofounded Aurora, and now lead product at GM.

Your new employer is betting the other way. A 2028 Cadillac Escalade IQ will launch eyes-off highway driving with cameras, radar and lidar all working together.

As I understand it, your case rests on four claims. Lidar helps camera systems learn faster, cameras can't see through dense fog, cameras can't measure instantaneous velocity the way radar can, and radar is so cheap that removing it makes no sense.

I agree that physics is real, and nobody at Tesla is pretending otherwise. What I'd like to show you is that Tesla's own engineering has been answering these exact points for years, and two of your arguments describe things Tesla already does.

A lot has also changed since you left. The in-house FSD computer arrived in 2019, camera-only Tesla Vision followed in 2021, and the end-to-end neural network that drives the car today came in 2024.

So let me take your physics one claim at a time.

🎓 ON LIDAR AS A TEACHER, TESLA HAS BEEN DOING THAT FOR YEARS

You said lidar works on a wavelength close to visible light, so it helps camera systems learn faster. You're right, and Tesla agrees so strongly that it built an entire training pipeline around that idea.

I like to think of lidar as a tutor holding a perfect answer key. It measures distance directly by timing laser pulses, so it can grade every guess a camera network makes about how far away something is.

Tesla has designed a system where a special test fleet carries radar and lidar alongside the regular cameras. Every reading is synchronized, so the precise depth and speed from the expensive sensors get attached automatically to the objects the cameras see.

The labeling even uses hindsight. When two cars blur into one blob early in a clip and separate later, the training servers rewind the footage and use the clear moment to label the confusing one correctly.

Tesla applies the same teacher to 3D space itself. Its occupancy network learns from lidar-backed ground truth to predict, for every small cube of space around the car, how far that cube sits from the nearest surface.

That's how plain cameras learn to sketch a sloped curb or a curved bumper smoothly instead of as a pile of blocky Lego bricks.

Even the grading got faster. Tesla designed a cross-labeling trick that draws a box around a car in a flat photo, then projects that box into the laser point cloud as a pyramid of vision, so the software only searches that slice instead of the whole 3D world.

You probably know DeepScale, the startup Tesla acquired in 2019. It was already working out in 2016 how to train cheap sensors to mimic premium lidar data, and Tesla is still pursuing that work today.

Here's the step where our views split.

Once the student has learned, the teacher can stay home. The test fleet keeps the expensive hardware, and the cars customers actually buy ship with cameras only.

Tesla has put real money behind this. In early 2024, lidar maker Luminar named Tesla its largest customer for the quarter, and Elon soon replied on X, "We don't need them even for that anymore."

The student is even learning to write its own answer key. To map the shape of the road surface, Tesla has designed a method that can triangulate ground truth points straight from camera images instead of relying on lidar.

Co-training requires lidar in the classroom, not in every car on the road. With respect, GM's plan keeps the teacher riding along forever.

⚡ ON SPEED, CAMERAS ARE QUICKER THAN THEY LOOK

Your sharpest point is about speed. Radar can measure how fast something is moving in a single snapshot, and a camera can't.

Radar's trick is the Doppler effect, the same physics that makes an ambulance siren sound higher as it rushes toward you and lower as it drives away. Radar reads that pitch shift in its own radio echo to measure closing speed instantly.

A camera has to work speed out from motion. It compares where an object sits in one frame with where it sits in the next, much like you judge a thrown ball by watching it fly.

That sounds slower, but the gap is tiny. Tesla's own designs describe cameras running at rates such as 36 frames per second, which puts a fresh frame in front of the network about every 28 milliseconds, quicker than a single blink.

The physics also cuts both ways. Doppler only measures motion toward or away from the sensor, so a car crossing your path sideways at an intersection produces little to no Doppler shift.

To catch that sideways motion, a radar has to track the car across several scans, which is exactly what a camera does with frames. On that kind of motion, the "instantaneous" advantage disappears.

Radar has another well-known weak spot. Owner's manuals for radar-based cruise control have long warned that the system may not brake for a stopped vehicle, partly because a parked car, an overhead sign and a bridge can all look like the same motionless metal.

Now here's what Tesla has built since you left.

Tesla has designed its vision network to output a full 3D velocity vector for every object, covering speed, direction and even height. It learned that skill from the radar on its test fleet, which turns ordinary cameras into something that behaves like a Doppler radar made of pixels.

Tesla's virtual camera invention goes further by measuring speed in two different ways. Cars are tracked relative to the moving Tesla itself, while pedestrians are tracked against the fixed ground, so the system knows a person's true walking path even while the car accelerates or turns.

When things get fast, the network speeds up its memory. A frame selector pulls video snapshots more rapidly as speeds rise and blends them with the car's own acceleration and yaw rate, which is how quickly the car is rotating, to build a smooth picture of motion over time.

There's also a dedicated sentinel for the car directly ahead. A super-narrow model watches only the closest vehicle in the lane through the narrowest forward lens and keeps estimating its distance, speed and acceleration, which is exactly what you need to brake hard and early.

So yes, a camera infers velocity instead of measuring it in one shot. But inference refreshed every few dozen milliseconds, trained on radar's own answers, and able to see sideways motion that Doppler misses is not a camera ignoring physics.

🌫️ ON FOG, I'LL GIVE YOU THAT ONE, BUT HEAR ME OUT

No camera sees through dense fog, and neither does the human eye. Radar does.

But look closely at your own argument. The near-visible wavelength that you said makes lidar a great teacher is the same reason lidar struggles in fog, because the tiny water droplets that scatter visible light also scatter laser light.

So the fog argument is really a radar argument, and radar alone can't finish the job. It can't read lane paint, a traffic light, a speed limit sign or a flagger's hand signal, so even a car loaded with radar still leans on its cameras when the world turns gray.

That's why I think the real question isn't whether a car can see through fog. The real question is whether the car knows when its vision is degraded, and whether it behaves like a careful driver when it is.

This is where Tesla's visibility invention comes in.

Tesla has designed a separate neural network whose only job is grading its own eyesight. It splits every camera feed into a fine grid and scores each cell from clear to blacked out, building a live heat map of where the car can and can't trust what it sees.

Each camera position gets its own specialist. A model judging the left pillar camera was trained on images from that same pillar location across many other cars, because a windshield camera behind wipers and a fender camera facing tire spray get dirty in very different ways.

The system also diagnoses the cause. It can tell a smear of mud from fog, heavy snow or a hardware fault, then reach for the right fix, such as running the wipers or warming the glass.

When a lens is blinded for a moment, the car doesn't forget the road. Tesla anchors what it saw to fixed spots in the physical world, so a pothole hidden by a truck's spray stays pinned on the car's mental map for those few seconds.

And when conditions really are too much, the car responds the way a good human driver would. It slows down to widen its reaction window, can move to a safer lane, and can hand control back with a plain explanation such as "Due to Heavy Snow, Autopilot is Reducing Speed."

Tesla is also sharpening the eyes themselves. Its designs feed raw, unprocessed sensor data straight into the AI chip, the same idea behind the "photon count" images Elon posted in May, when he said this is why FSD can see so well at night or through extreme glare.

Around the lens, Tesla has designed micro-cone glare shields, corrective windshield patches, pulsed laser cleaning and even gas-absorbing plastics that keep a hazy chemical film off the inside of the glass. Each one attacks a different way a camera can lose its view.

Fog will always be fog. Tesla's bet is a car that measures how blind it is, remembers what it saw, and slows down exactly when a wise driver would.

💸 YES, RADAR IS CHEAP, BUT THAT WAS NEVER THE POINT

You're right that a radar unit doesn't cost much. But Elon's case against it was never about the sticker price.

In April 2021, as Tesla prepared to remove radar, Elon explained it this way: "Sensors are a bitstream and cameras have several orders of magnitude more bits/sec than radar (or lidar)." A second sensor, he added, has to meaningfully improve the signal to be worth the complexity of integrating it.

In August 2025 he put it even more bluntly: "Lidar and radar reduce safety due to sensor contention. If lidars/radars disagree with cameras, which one wins?" In the same post, he wrote that Tesla turned off the radars in its cars to increase safety.

Picture two witnesses to the same moment telling different stories. The radar reports a solid object ahead, the cameras see an empty road under a steel overpass, and the car has a fraction of a second to decide who's wrong.

Trust the radar every time and you get phantom braking under bridges. Trust the cameras every time and the radar was only along for the ride.

Then there's the cost that never shows up on a parts list. Every extra sensor needs calibration, its own data pipeline, fusion software and validation for every way the sensors can disagree, and that burden grows with each new sensor type.

Tesla's own history shows how heavy that lift is. The DeepScale design for mimicking lidar needed separate neural branches for each sensor type just to absorb their different quirks, timing and mounting positions before merging them.

I'd argue the biggest hidden cost is data. Tesla's FSD (Supervised) fleet has logged more than 16.7 billion miles, nearly all of it seen through cameras alone, and a radar channel added today would arrive with none of that history to learn from.

Look at what happened at Volvo this summer. In July, the company confirmed it was dropping lidar from the EX90 and ES90 after cutting ties with its supplier Luminar, which went bankrupt, and Norwegian owners are receiving NOK 18,000 per car for lidar features that never arrived.

Elon's reply was short: "I did try to warn them. Humans drive using neural nets and optical sensors. Same is true for robot cars."

Cheap hardware can turn into an expensive argument, and back in 2021 Tesla decided it would rather not have the argument at all.

🛣️ WHILE YOUR SYSTEM WAITS FOR 2028, CAMERA-ONLY TESLAS ARE ALREADY LOGGING THE MILES

Your plan for handing control back deserves real credit. You said the Escalade won't toss the wheel to a surprised driver, and will instead give a countdown of around ten minutes and pull off at an exit if nobody takes over.

That philosophy should sound familiar, because Tesla's visibility invention describes the same graceful exit. The car slows down first, looks for a safer lane, explains the reason on the screen, and only then hands control back.

The real difference is timing. GM's eyes-off system is still a 2028 promise, while Tesla's camera-only cars are collecting evidence right now.

Tesla's latest FSD (Supervised) safety report shows 6,006,200 miles per major collision in North America, compared with a U.S. average of 660,164 miles. That's roughly nine times as far between airbag-level crashes, measured over a rolling twelve months.

Tesla's new Robotaxi safety report goes a step further. Driverless Teslas with no safety monitor inside have covered 3.1 million miles in Texas and Florida this year, including 862,000 miles after dark and 113,000 miles in rain, with zero people injured by a Robotaxi and zero airbag deployments, based on the crash reports Tesla files with NHTSA.

And that Robotaxi fleet runs on the latest Model Y and the Cybercab, neither of which carries radar or lidar. I find that hard to square with the idea that camera-only driving ignores physics.

🔭 WHERE I THINK WE REALLY DISAGREE

You framed this as physics versus faith, but I think both sides accept the same physics. What we really disagree about is where the intelligence should live.

GM puts more of it in the hardware, stacking sensors so each one covers another's weak spot. Tesla puts it in the neural network, using radar and lidar as teachers in the classroom and then trusting a trained brain behind the cameras.

There's a quiet twist hidden in that choice. A multi-sensor car can only learn from fleets that carry the same sensors, while every camera-equipped Tesla on the road feeds the same classroom.

Physics decides what a sensor can see. Data decides what a car understands.

Best regards,

Ming

P.S. If you're ever in Austin, a driverless Tesla might make my case better than I can, and it won't need lidar to find you.

$CNX | @crynuxio might be one of the more overlooked projects in the decentralized AI sector.

55 million tasks completed during testnet.

1,785 participating nodes.

A working AI chat and image-generation application.

And 71% of $CNX supply allocated to task mining tied to network usage.

Here’s why I’ve been paying attention 🔽

1️⃣ Turning idle GPUs into productive infrastructure

There are millions of GPUs sitting inside gaming PCs and other computers around the world.

Many of them remain underutilized for significant portions of the day.

Crynux is building a decentralized network that allows GPU owners to contribute their computing resources to AI workloads.

Instead of relying entirely on centralized infrastructure providers, developers can access computational power supplied by independent operators.

The arrangement is straightforward:

→ GPU owners contribute computing power.

→ Developers use that power to run AI applications.

→ Operators earn $CNX for completing tasks.

The interesting part is that a computer in one part of the world can process an AI request originating from an application thousands of kilometres away.

And the network handles the coordination.

2️⃣ But does decentralized AI actually work?

This was the question I wanted answered.

A decentralized computing network sounds promising in theory, but the real test is whether it can deliver something people can actually use.

That’s where Crynux Chat comes in.

It’s a working AI application powered by the Crynux network, with a free demo that anyone can explore.

You can interact with AI models, ask questions, generate content, and even create images.

For example, one of the demonstrations involves generating an image of a small red lighthouse on a snowy cliff at dusk.

Here’s what happens behind the scenes.

When you submit the prompt:

→ Crynux-AS submits the task to the network.

→ The blockchain assigns an available GPU node.

→ The node receives the task through a relay and runs the AI model.

→ The network performs the required validation.

→ The generated image returns to your chat.

And you can actually follow the progress.

The interface shows the different stages: In Queue, Generating, Verifying, Uploading, and Finishing.

The example uses Qwen Image 2.1, with the actual computation performed by a GPU node participating in the network.

It’s a simple demonstration, but it makes the underlying technology much easier to understand.

3️⃣ Solving the trust problem

Now comes one of the more interesting technical challenges.

If anyone can contribute hardware, how does the network know that operators are completing tasks correctly?

After all, decentralized infrastructure can’t simply assume every participant is honest.

Crynux addresses this through its verification system, vssML.

Rather than duplicating every computation, the network uses unpredictable checks.

Approximately 10% of tasks are selected for independent verification, with results compared across three nodes.

Operators don’t know beforehand which tasks will be checked.

And because they have $CNX at stake, submitting dishonest results carries financial consequences.

The objective is to make dishonest behaviour economically unattractive while avoiding the enormous cost of independently repeating every computation.

4️⃣ More than just AI chatbots

Crynux Chat is one application built on the network, but the potential use cases extend considerably further.

The infrastructure supports workloads involving:

→ AI chatbots and virtual assistants

→ Text generation, translation, and summarization

→ Code generation and debugging

→ AI image generation and editing

→ Model fine-tuning

→ LoRA training and customization

For developers, another important feature is compatibility with familiar AI development tools and request formats.

That means existing applications can potentially integrate Crynux without rebuilding their entire AI infrastructure.

And this is important because the easier it becomes for developers to access decentralized computing, the easier it becomes for the network to attract real workloads.

5️⃣ The $CNX economics are particularly interesting

This is one aspect I think deserves more attention.

71% of the maximum $CNX supply is allocated to task mining.

But unlike conventional token emission schedules, these allocations are linked to network demand and completed work.

In other words, the task-mining allocation isn’t simply released because another month has passed.

Actual network activity drives its distribution.

Why does this matter?

Because many crypto projects experience supply expansion regardless of whether their products attract meaningful adoption.

Crynux takes a different approach with its task-mining allocation.

Of course, this doesn’t eliminate dilution altogether. Other token allocations and circulating supply dynamics still matter.

But linking a substantial portion of token distribution to actual computational work creates an interesting relationship between network usage and token issuance.

It’s a model worth watching as adoption develops.

6️⃣ Where does Crynux stand today?

Crynux launched its mainnet in June 2026.

Before that, its testnet recorded:

→ 1,785 participating nodes

→ 55 million completed tasks

Those figures provide some early evidence of network activity, although sustained mainnet usage will ultimately be the more important measure.

There’s also a fairly accessible way for newcomers to explore the ecosystem.

Crynux Chat offers a free demo with a limited daily allowance.

Users can try AI conversations and image generation without immediately needing to purchase tokens.

Wallet connectivity is optional for users who want to access their own Crynux credits.

One important detail: conversations are stored locally in the browser, and GPU node operators may have access to the information necessary to process requests. Sensitive information should therefore never be submitted.

✦ My perspective

I’ve always been more interested in crypto projects that build technology people have a practical reason to use.

And decentralized AI computing is an area I believe deserves serious attention.

The demand for AI computation is real. The hardware needed to supply it already exists.

The opportunity lies in connecting those resources efficiently, making the computation reliable, and building an ecosystem that developers actually want to use.

That’s the opportunity Crynux is pursuing.

The next questions are whether the network can attract sustained developer demand, remain cost-competitive, and scale reliably.

Those are the metrics I’ll be paying attention to.

For now, @crynuxio is firmly on my radar.
